ideas.canonical_en: The Great Molasses Flood of Boston in 1919
ideas.question: Ek shehar mein sirop ki lehar aayi aur sadkon par tabahi macha di, ye sach hai?
ideas.hook: Ek din Boston ki sadkon par meetha sirop ki lehar aayi, aur 21 log mar gaye.
ideas.angle: A funny-sounding setup with a dark ending, plus the physics of why cold syrup is deadly.

ideas.canonical_en: Why do you suddenly need to pee more when it's cold?
ideas.question: सर्दी में बार-बार पेशाब क्यों लगता है, जबकि पानी भी कम पीते हैं?
ideas.hook: सर्दी में पानी कम पीते हो, फिर भी बाथरूम के चक्कर क्यों बढ़ जाते हैं?
ideas.angle: Cold diuresis: the body is not pushing out extra water. It is protecting your core by moving blood around.

ideas.canonical_en: Why shooting stars are mostly the size of a grain of sand and what makes them glow
ideas.question: Why does a grain of sand light up the whole night sky?
ideas.hook: That streak across the sky? It's usually a speck the size of a grain of sand.
ideas.angle: Meteors glow because of air compressed in front of the grain, not friction. Tie it to the Leonid meteor shower, which peaks around Nov 17-18.

ideas.canonical_en: Why do the Leonid meteor showers sometimes turn into meteor storms with thousands of shooting stars per hour?
ideas.question: Why did the sky once rain 100,000 meteors an hour, and could it happen again?
ideas.hook: In 1966, the night sky over Arizona rained about 40 meteors every single second.
ideas.angle: Covers the comet's dust trails and the 33-year cycle behind the rare Leonid storms (1833, 1966, 1999-2002), not how a shooting star glows. It's timed to this week's peak on Nov 17-18.

ideas.canonical_en: Why does a glacier in Antarctica bleed blood-red water?
ideas.question: Why is there a glacier in Antarctica that looks like it's bleeding?
ideas.hook: In Antarctica there's a glacier that bleeds. And the 'blood' comes out clear.
ideas.angle: The red is not algae, as explorers once guessed. It is very salty, iron-rich water from a lake that has been sealed under the ice for over a million years. The water comes out clear and only turns red when it meets air, the same way iron rusts. Microbes live down there in total darkness by 'breathing' iron.

ideas.canonical_en: Why the scariest pirate in history may never have killed anyone until his last fight
ideas.question: Did Blackbeard actually kill anyone, or was the smoking beard the whole trick?
ideas.hook: The most feared pirate in history set his own beard on fire, and that may be why he never had to kill anyone.
ideas.angle: Blackbeard as a branding genius. It was psychological warfare: slow-burning fuses under his hat and a terrifying image, so ships surrendered without a fight. Historians find no reliable record of him killing anyone before his final battle on November 22, 1718.

ideas.canonical_en: How could a whale sink a whaling ship on purpose (the Essex, Nov 20, 1820)?
ideas.question: How did a whale sink a ship on purpose?
ideas.hook: This week in 1820, a whale looked at a ship, swam away, turned around and rammed it. Twice.
ideas.angle: This uses the anniversary to explain the whale's head. Its front third is a giant oil-filled sonar organ sitting on top of the 'junk', a stack of tissue that works like a shock absorber. Studies suggest males may use it as a battering ram on each other.

ideas.canonical_en: Why did America have two different Thanksgivings in 1939?
ideas.question: How did one country end up eating Thanksgiving dinner on two different Thursdays?
ideas.hook: In 1939, America had two Thanksgivings, one week apart.
ideas.angle: The cause was not religion or tradition. It was shopping. November 1939 had five Thursdays, retailers feared a short Christmas season, and FDR moved the holiday. States split, families split, and the joke name was 'Franksgiving'.

ideas.canonical_en: Did tulip mania really bankrupt the Dutch, or is the famous bubble mostly a myth?
ideas.question: Did the famous tulip bubble really make people go broke?
ideas.hook: History's craziest bubble bankrupted nobody we can find.
ideas.angle: A versus of the legend and the archives. The legend, popularized in an 1841 book: chimney sweeps trading houses for bulbs, then the whole country ruined. The archives, as historian Anne Goldgar found: buyers were mostly wealthy merchants, she found no bankruptcy caused by tulips, and the real damage was broken promises and reputations. Prices really did spike and crash in Feb 1637.
